four_oclock_door.title: The Four O'Clock Door
four_oclock_door.summary: Noor needs a pair of hands that can wake. The interview is a dawn, a dropped tray, and a basket she has sent out one loaf short on purpose.

card.log: Talk to Noor at the Stone Oven, Baker Street

n_again.say: You again. The card's still in the window, I notice. Same morning, same basket, same test. I don't change a test because somebody failed it. Four o'clock. Side door.

n1.say: We're closed. We've been closed since the bread ran out, which was ten past nine. The card says early.

options.text: The card says you need a pair of hands.
You sell out by nine and you want more help?
Mei at the Tram Café sent me.

n2.say: Everyone has hands. I need ones that show up. The last pair came attached to a nice boy and a phone. The phone showed up more.

lastone.say: The mall happened. Shiny counter, nine o'clock start, music in the ceiling. He's happier. His bread isn't.

options.text: I'm not here for the music.

nine.say: No. It sounds comfortable. Bread doesn't rise on comfortable. The mall is four hundred metres that way.

mei.say: Mei doesn't send me people. She sends me orders and gossip, in that order. She says you gave her your own loaf. That's either foolish or promising.

justbread.say: No such thing. That's the first wrong thing you've said. Say the rest after four tomorrow.

cheek.say: It's not more I want. It's the same, done right, with two of us standing up. You've a tongue on you. The oven doesn't care about tongues.

early.say: Four. The oven doesn't do lie-ins. Side door, in the alley. Knock like you mean it. If you're awake, you'll do.

four.say: There's another four? The mall's pastry counter opens at nine, I'm told. Perhaps that's more your hour.

dawn.log: Be at the bakery's side door between 03:50 and 04:20

morning.log: Work the dawn shift, and deal with what Pip drops

f1.say: Coat on the hook. Hands under the tap. You knead what I give you, you weigh what you shape, and you don't touch the jar on the top shelf.

crock2.say: Everything in this room is flour, water, salt and time. The jar is mostly time. You get the time when you've earned the flour.

teach.say: Shoulders, not wrists. The dough can tell when you're lying. Push it away like you mean it. Fold it back like you're sorry. Again.

cellar.say: Ten past five. Noor goes down to the cellar for salt. Ninety seconds later the side door bangs and Pip arrives at a dead run, coat half on, and catches the proving rack with one elbow. A tray of seeded loaves, proved all night, goes face down on the flags.

options.text: (Look at the tray. Look at Pip.)

pip1.say: No, no, no. The seeded batch. Those took all night. She'll turn me into rusks. You didn't see this. Did you see this?

options.text: Reshape them, fast. I'll watch the stairs.
We tell her. Now. Both of us, together.
(Call down the stairs.) Noor! Tray down!

cover.say: You'd do that? For me? Right. Watch the stairs. They'll bake flat, but market-day people don't look. They just want the seeds.

cover2.say: Thanks. I owe you one. I'm already carrying one I owe. They stack, apparently.

cover3.say: Nothing. Nobody. Ask me when something's on fire. I'm more honest when something's on fire.

hm.dir: She comes back up with the salt and looks at the seeded trays for one second longer than necessary.

together.say: Together? Nobody says together in a kitchen. It's always one person's fault. That's what kitchens are for.

together2.say: Burns get shown, not hidden. Same with trays. Reshape, prove again, and the pair of you owe me an hour of pastry. Ashby. You said “we”. Noted.
together2.dir: She looks at the tray, then at the two of you standing shoulder to shoulder like a court martial.

report.dir: She comes up slowly, looks at the tray, then at Pip for a long moment, then at you.

options.text: It seemed like you should know.

report2.say: No, it's fine. It's fine. Welcome to the Stone Oven. Mind the rack. It bites.

barrow.say: Twelve for the Tram Café. Six for Market Grocer. Before the seven o'clock tram. That one's yours. Breakfast. Don't eat it walking.
barrow.dir: Half past six. She loads the barrow herself, then tucks a smaller, darker loaf into your coat pocket. One seeded loaf in brown paper stays behind on the rack, with a chalk cross on it and no name.

count.log: Push the barrow to Market Square before the seven o'clock tram

c1.say: Halfway down Baker Street you count the barrow, because she told you to weigh what you shape, and a count is a kind of weighing. Seventeen. The café's twelve and the grocer's six make eighteen. Nobody is watching. The tram is due in nine minutes.

options.text: Go back and tell Noor the count is wrong.
The café gets its twelve. The grocer gets five and an apology.
The grocer gets his six. The café gets eleven and an apology.
The mall sells bread. Nobody needs to know.

back.say: You counted. Good. You are also now eleven minutes behind the tram. Run.
back.dir: She is waiting at the side door with the eighteenth loaf already in her hand.

mall.say: Eastgate Mall, at a run. One counter has its shutters half up. A man with a retail smile sells you a white loaf that is warm, even, and smells of nothing at all. “Emergency?” he says. “We get a lot of emergencies.” You tuck it among the grocer's six.

cafe.log: Deliver to Mei at the Tram Café

m_full.say: Twelve, warm, and before the tram! The Oven's found a barrow that can tell the time. How is she? Is she being nice? Don't answer that. She's never nice. She's better than nice.

options.text: Better than nice. That's about it.

m_mall.say: Twelve, warm, and only just. The tram has been in two minutes and they were starting to circle. Where have you been? Don't answer. Go. The grocer's waiting.

m_gift.say: Twelve! Warm! And hang on. One of these is darker. That's a baker's own loaf. That's your breakfast, isn't it?

options.text: A loaf is a loaf, Mei.
A loaf is a loaf, Mei.

m_gift2.say: That's twice now. The bread thing. You know that's twice? I'm telling Noor. Loudly. While she pretends not to listen.

m_gift2b.say: You put your own breakfast in my basket. Nobody does that. I'm telling Noor. Loudly. While she pretends not to listen.

m_late.say: Eleven minutes! I have had a tram full of people looking at an empty basket for eleven minutes. Do you know what a tram full of people looks like?

options.text: The count was short. I went back for the twelfth.

m_late2.say: You went back. Most would have handed me eleven and a face. Fine. Forgiven. Mostly. Go, the grocer's waiting.

options.text: It's eleven today. My count, my fault. I'm sorry.

m_short2.say: Honest and short. Like my favourite people. The tram crowd will take what's here and argue with the air about the rest. Go on.

m_short3.say: Blaming Noor's arithmetic. Brave. Wrong, I expect, but brave. Go on.

grocer.log: Deliver to Olu at Market Grocer

o_full.say: Six on the nail, still warm. Tell Noor the bet stands. She'll know.

o_bet.say: Nine years ago I bet her a sweet roll she couldn't go one year without a day off. Nine years that bet has rolled over. The interest alone is a bakery.

o_short.say: Five. The café gets her twelve and I get five and, what, a story?

options.text: Five and an apology. The short count is mine.

o_short2.say: A story with an apology in it. I can sell that. It'll cost you, mind. I'll be telling it for a week.

o_short3.say: And my shelf can? My shelf has feelings. Tell Noor the bet stands, and tell her I counted.

o_mall.say: Six. On time. Tell Noor the bet stands.
o_mall.dir: He lifts the loaves out one at a time. At the fifth he stops, turns it over, and looks at you for exactly as long as it takes to decide to say nothing.

v1.dir: The order book lies open between you. The recent entries are in a rounder hand than the pages before.
v1.covered: The count scene always leaves one of its five facts before the line reaches Noor.

options.text: We were one short. I put my own loaf in.
I counted, and I came back. You know the rest.
One short. I shorted the grocer.
One short. I shorted the café.
The count was short. I bought a mall loaf to cover it.
Whose writing is that in the order book?

v_book.say: Pip's. Pip keeps the book these days. My pen and I are not speaking. The round.

v_gift.say: I know. I shorted the basket myself. Eighteen owed, seventeen sent. You could have blamed me, blamed Pip, or bought your way out. You gave away your breakfast.

v_why.say: I short every first basket. It's the cheapest honest look at a person that money can buy. One loaf.

v_count.say: You did. Eleven minutes late and one count right. A count you check is yours. A count you don't is mine, and I am tired of carrying everybody's.

v_short.say: And you told them so? To their face?

options.text: To their face. More or less.

v_short2.say: Then here is the lesson, free. There was no right one to short. Olu's shelf is money, Mei's tram is noise, and both of them are mine. I shorted the basket myself. I wanted to hear whether you would tell me which.

v_short_blame.say: More or less. Mei tells me you said it was my count. It was. You didn't know that when you said it. Side door key. It works until it doesn't.

v_confess.say: I know. Olu has a good eye and a better mouth. This rose in a steel tray, in a warm cupboard, four hundred metres from my oven. And it wore my basket to do it.
v_confess.dir: She reaches under the counter and sets a loaf between you. White. Even. Olu brought it round an hour ago.

options.text: I panicked. It won't happen again.
Nobody went short. Isn't that the job?

v_lie.say: Full count. Then explain this one. Olu brought it round an hour ago. It rose in a steel tray, in a warm cupboard, and it wore my basket.
v_lie.dir: She reaches under the counter and sets a loaf between you. White. Even.

options.text: I'm sorry. I should have told you first.
The order was filled, wasn't it?

v_wary_lie.say: Yes. You should. Wrong twice before breakfast: once at the mall, and once to my face. Side door key. It works until it doesn't.

v_wary.say: No, it won't. Because from now on you'll count. Side door key. It works until it doesn't. Understand me?

v_brazen.say: The job is the bread. Go and fill orders somewhere that can't taste the difference. The mall's hiring. Tell them I sent you. They'll enjoy that.

v_key.say: Sit. Eat. Side door. There are three of those keys in the world. Four o'clock tomorrow. Don't be early. Early people are as much trouble as late ones.
v_key.dir: She pushes a dark loaf across the counter, the twin of the one in your pocket this morning, and sets a key beside it as if it were a teaspoon.

options.text: About the seeded batch this morning...

v_pip.say: Rose flat. Reshaped in a hurry. Seeds pressed on after. I counted the trays before the cellar and after. You covered for someone you had known a minute. That's a kind heart and a cheap one. Today was your one blind eye. Spend the next one better.

hired_clean.title: Hired, clean
hired_clean.log: Noor handed you the side-door key as if it were nothing. There are three in the world.

hired_wary.title: Hired, on watch
hired_wary.log: The key, but not the nod. Noor is counting you now, the way she counts the change.

turned_away.title: The door stays shut
turned_away.log: “Go and fill orders somewhere that can't taste the difference.” The card stays in the window. You can knock again tomorrow.

feeding_the_mother.title: Feeding the Mother
feeding_the_mother.summary: A power cut has chilled the Mother, the bakery's 120-year-old sourdough culture, and she has gone still. Saving her takes the old stoneware crock from the museum, rye from the last stone mill, and a night's vigil. There is also a second way: a jam jar in a mall fridge, labelled MUM, that nobody was ever meant to know about.

still.log: Talk to Noor at the Stone Oven

s1.say: She's not bubbling. Fed at midnight, fed at five. Nothing. The heater went off with the power, and she went cold.

options.text: It's only starter. We could grow a new one in a week.

she.say: The Mother. My great-grandmother started her the week they pulled the wall down. Every loaf this shop has ever sold came off her. You've been eating her since you came.

options.text: Then let's wake her. What does she need?

only.say: A new one would make bread. It would not make our bread. You can get a new dog, too.

options.text: I'm sorry. Tell me what she needs.

only2.say: No. That was unfair. You weren't to know. Nobody's to know. That is half my trouble this morning.

plan.say: Warmth that doesn't swing. The old stoneware crock held heat like a grudge; this glass thing holds nothing. Fresh rye, stone-ground. She won't take roller flour, never has. And a night of feeding. The crock is in the museum. The rye is Oda's, at Mill Fields.

options.text: Why is your crock in a museum?

why.say: Jai has it under glass with a little card. “Bread crock, Stone Oven Bakery.” As if it had finished doing things. Ask him. I don't go in there.

crock.log: Get the stoneware crock from the Old Town Museum

j1.say: Come to see the token drawer? I've put it in order of year.

options.text: Not today, Jai. I need the bakery crock. OT-112.

j2.say: The Stone Oven crock? It's accessioned. Releasing an object needs form D-7, signed by the donor. The donor is Noor. I do have the form. I have all the forms.

options.text: Give me the form. She'll sign.
Couldn't it go out on loan? Museums lend things.
Jai, the bakery's culture is dying. Tonight.
Forget the crock. Blankets will do.

j_loan.say: Loans go to the committee, and the committee is Mrs Ellery's kitchen table on the first Thursday. Unless. An object may return to use for “demonstration of original function”. I should have to see it work. I should very much like to see it work.

options.text: Come and watch bread happen, Jai.
A signed form is cleaner. Give me the D-7.

j_loan2.say: OT-112, outgoing, demonstration of original function. I want to hear what a crock sounds like when it isn't an exhibit.
j_loan2.dir: He wraps the crock in acid-free paper like a christening.

j_press.say: Tonight. Of course it's tonight. It's always tonight with living things. That is why I work with objects. The form is proper. The loan is possible. Please don't choose the third thing you're thinking.

options.text: The form. I'll take it to Noor.
The loan. Come and watch it work.
(At closing, lift the crock into your barrow.)

j_take.say: The case is not locked. A museum like this trusts you; that is most of the exhibit. The crock rides home under a flour sack. The little card stays behind, face down, as if it couldn't watch.

j_thief.say: You. I have a gap on a shelf where a first edition should be, and now you want to borrow something else?

options.text: I brought the book back, Jai.
The bakery's culture is dying. This isn't about me.

j_back.say: You brought it back. Well. The shelf has been wrong for weeks. I had started walking the long way round it. Thank you. Now. What was it you needed?

j_thief2.say: No. It isn't. Which is why you may have the proper form and nothing else. D-7, donor's signature. Rules are for exactly the people I can't trust.

options.text: (At closing, lift the crock into your barrow.)
Forget the crock. Blankets will do.

g1.say: I signed her away the week my mother died. Grief does strange paperwork. You give away the one thing you're going to need.
g1.dir: She reads the form twice. Her pen stops over the donor line of the old receipt stapled behind it, where her own signature sits, six years younger.

options.text: Sign it, Noor. The crock's coming home.

g2.say: Tell Jai it was looked after there. He'll want to hear that. He labels things so they'll be remembered. It isn't his fault that I wanted to forget.
g2.dir: She signs. It costs her something you can watch leaving.

options.text: (Take the signed form back to Jai, tell him so, and carry the crock home.)

rye.log: Get stone-ground rye from Oda at Mill Fields

o1.say: Stone Oven barrow, new face. Let me guess. The Mother's taken a chill and Noor wants rye.
o1.dir: She listens to the mill over your shoulder the whole time she talks to you.

options.text: That's the size of it. Fresh ground, she said.

o_how.say: Forty years of her. Rye is the nurse of the grains. Wheat's the patient; rye sits up all night. When the Stone Oven sends for rye in a hurry, somebody's poorly.

o_grind.say: Fresh means now, and now means you turn the small stone with me. Mind your sleeve.

o_knock.say: The small stone turns. The flour comes off cool and grey and sweet. Twice in the turning, the big mill behind you knocks: a dull, wrong note, like a cough in a singer.

o_dull.say: The big stones, going dull. A stone talks while it's cutting right. This one's been mumbling for a year now. They want dressing, and the man who dressed them isn't available.

o_marek.say: Marek. My husband. Two years gone. His tools went to the museum because I couldn't have them in the house. One patient at a time. Rye first.

o_water.say: Here. And tell Noor what she already knows, because tonight she'll be too tired to know it. Wrist-warm water. Never the kettle. Cold only slows a culture down. Hot kills her dead.

pip.log: Bring the rye back to the Stone Oven

p1.say: You got the rye? Good. Listen. Something's on fire, so I'm being honest. There's another one. Another Mother.

p2.say: Tam. Noor's brother, at the mall. He offered me a job and I went to hear it, don't look at me like that. In his back fridge there's a jam jar. Labelled MUM. He feeds it every day. Like a goldfish.

options.text: You went to hear a job offer from Tam?
A cutting of the Mother. Alive.

p3.say: Double the wage and a nine o'clock start. I haven't said yes. I haven't said no. That's what I've been carrying about. Now you're carrying it too. Sorry.

options.text: One fire at a time. The jar.

p4.say: If she won't wake, his will. Same culture, six years apart. But if Noor finds out where it came from, I don't know what she does. I honestly don't.

options.text: No. We do this Noor's way.

p_cold.say: Rye goes on the bench. Noor says the vigil starts at eleven.

options.text: Pip. Is there anything else I should know?

p_cold2.say: You'd only report it. Fine. It's bigger than me being cross. Tam, Noor's brother, at the mall, keeps a cutting of the Mother in his fridge. Labelled MUM. Do what you like with that. You usually do.

jar.log: Optional: ask Tam at Crumb & Co, Eastgate Mall

t1.say: Welcome to Crumb and Co, where the bread is warm and the lighting is warmer! What can I get you?

t_emergency.say: Hang on, I know you. Emergency white, at the crack of dawn! How was the emergency?

options.text: It went into your sister's basket.

t_emergency2.say: You put one of my loaves in Noor's basket? That is the funniest thing that has ever happened to me, and I can't tell a soul. She caught you, of course.

t2.say: You're hers. The new one. Did she send you?
t2.dir: The patter stops like a dropped tray. He is looking at the flour on your sleeves.

options.text: No. She doesn't know I'm here.

t_lie.say: No, she doesn't. If Noor sent for help, the fountain would hand in its notice. Try again, and leave the sales pitch out. I write three a day.

options.text: She doesn't know. The Mother's dying.

t_truth.say: Course she doesn't. Come through the back. If you're here and she doesn't know, it's bad. And if it's bad, it's the Mother.
t_truth.dir: He flips the counter sign to CLOSED with a flourish that has nothing behind it.

t_dying.say: Six years I've kept her alive in there. Fed her before stock-take, every day. I told myself it was insurance. Insurance against exactly this.
t_dying.dir: He takes a jam jar down from the back fridge. MUM, in marker, gone brown at the edges.

options.text: Give me a cup of it. Please.
Why keep it secret for six years?
A courier brings a seeded loaf here every Saturday. That's you.

t_why.say: Because I took it without asking, and every day since has made the first day worse. There's a maths to owing people. My sister invented it. And the funny part: the mall won't let me bake with it. “Non-standard input.” Nobody laughs at that part.

options.text: Give me a cup of it. For her.

t_loaf.say: Abe wouldn't have told you. You worked it out. One seeded loaf, every Saturday, six years. I have never once eaten my own bread on a Saturday. Don't tell her that. Tell her anything else.

options.text: Give me a cup of it, Tam.

t_self.say: Walk up Baker Street with a jam jar and six years of silence? She'd close the shutters. No. Worse. She'd be polite. You take it. You've got clean hands.

t_ask.say: One condition, and you pick it. Who tells her where this came from?
t_ask.dir: He spoons it into a clean jar like a transfusion.

options.text: Nobody. She never finds out. It's kinder.
On second thought, keep it. We'll do this her way.

t_price_truth.say: Huh. I'd budgeted for the other answer. Then tell her it was fed. Every day. Whatever else she thinks of me, it was fed every day.

t_price_secret.say: Kinder. Right. Kind the way the mall is warm. Take it. Saturdays, if anyone asks, you never met me.

t_refuse.say: Her way. It's always her way. That's not a complaint, it's a description. The jar's here if her way runs out.

vigil.log: Keep the vigil at the Stone Oven from 23:00

v0.say: Eleven at night. The old crock sits in the oven's afterglow, fed with rye and wrist-warm water, stirred with the handle end of a wooden spoon, because that is how she has always been stirred and tonight is not the night for progress.

options.text: (Sit down. It's a long time till five.)

v0_glass.say: Eleven at night. The glass jar sits by the oven door, wrapped in two blankets and Noor's cardigan. It looks like a patient. The glass is already cool to the touch.

v1.say: My great-grandmother started her the week the wall came down. Everyone was starting something that week. A shop, a marriage, an argument. A culture was cheaper than a baby, and she has outlasted most of the marriages. Talk to me. It's a long time till five.

options.text: Noor. I have something of hers. From Tam.

v_mother.say: She could tell the weather from the crumb. Rain two days out. Hands like paper at the end, and she'd still catch me adding yeast on a slow morning. Not angry. Disappointed. Which, as you know, is the strong one.

options.text: And Tam? Was he here then?

v_tam.say: My brother wanted lights. A till that sings. Our name over six counters in six towns. I wanted the oven. We were both right. That's the trouble with bread. It proves slow, and people won't. He left on a Tuesday. I opened on time.

options.text: Have you ever walked past his counter?
Noor. About Tam. I have something.

v_counter.say: Once. From the far side. He was laughing with a customer. Good laugh, my brother. Retail laugh now. It started out real.

options.text: Noor. I went to see him today.

v_reveal.say: He took a cutting. And he fed it? Six years, in that place?
v_reveal.dir: You set a clean jam jar on the table, with a cupful of culture in it. She looks at it for a long time without touching it.

options.text: Every day. He asked me to tell you that. Every day.
Every day. I promised him I'd say nothing. I'm saying it anyway.

v_told.say: Six years I let him be a till with a haircut. And all that time he was feeding her. Same sour. Same stubborn. Then it's still the same bread. Fold it in.
v_told.dir: She sits down. Noor, who stands through everything, sits down. Then she opens the jar and smells it.

v_two.say: Two o'clock, and a feed. Then the long hour. Somewhere after three Noor falls asleep in the chair with her hands folded under her arms, the way people hold something that hurts. Four o'clock. The feed is yours.

v_four.say: Rye on the bench. The tap runs wrist-warm if you wait for it. The kettle has just boiled for Noor's tea, the hour is very late, and hot would surely be quicker.

v_wake.say: You woke me to ask. Good. Asking is cheaper than guessing. Wrist-warm. Handle end. Watch.

v_right_noor.say: She feeds the culture herself, wrist-warm, handle end, and does not go back to sleep. A little before five a bubble rises through the grey, slow as a word remembered. Then another.

v_cold_noor.say: The feed's right, and it isn't enough. The glass gives the heat away as fast as the oven lends it. I should never have let that crock out of the house.

options.text: Noor. There's another one. Tam kept a cutting alive, and I have it here.

v_told_late.say: He kept a cutting. Six years. And you have sat there with it in your pocket all night while she died in front of me. Give it here. Handle end. Fold it in.

v_cold.say: The feed is right, and it isn't enough. The glass gives the heat away as fast as the oven lends it. By half past four the surface is as flat and grey as it was at midnight.

morning.log: Five o'clock at the Stone Oven

w_pure.say: Stubborn. Like her keeper. Here. Proofing room key. There are two of those in the world.
w_pure.dir: She lifts the lid. The Mother is loud this morning, frothing at the shoulder of the crock as if making up for lost time.

options.text: (Take the key. Tam's jar goes back to Eastgate, unopened.)

w_join.say: Six years apart, and she takes him back in a night. No argument. No sulk. She's a better family than the rest of us. Proofing room key. And Ashby. On Saturday the seeded loaf goes to Eastgate with the morning round. On the books. No more cash.

w_secret.say: She's risen. She's rounder. As if she's been somewhere. Hm. Sleep does that. Proofing room key.
w_secret.dir: She tastes the culture off the back of the spoon and holds it on her tongue a moment too long.

options.text: Noor. She has been somewhere. Tam kept a cutting.

w_late.say: And you'd have let me think it was the rye. No. Don't explain. You told me before the shutters went up. That counts. It only just counts.

s_in_table.say: Stand up straight. Both of you. Married at the Town Oven, with the fire lit. I queued on this spot at eight years old with a token in my mitten, and I never thought to see it used for this. Eli. Your clipboard.

s_ring.say: Eli finds her place on the form. Beside you, somebody is patting every pocket they own.
s_ring.covered: Eli's clipboard always leaves one of the four best-person facts before the square.

ring_pip.say: I've got it. I've checked it over and over. It's in the pocket with the plectrum. No. The other pocket. I've got it.

ring_abe.say: One ring, signed for, on time. First thing I have ever carried that I'd have paid to carry.

ring_tam.say: I'm holding the ring at a wedding my sister baked for. If I drop it, she'll count that too.

ring_olu.say: I have the ring. I have also a few words about how I introduced the two of you. No? After, then.

s_eli.say: By the power of this clipboard, and of the Town Hall, who lent me the stamp. You first. Say what you came to say.

options.text: I'll be there at five past twelve. Every day, for as long as there are days.
I'll keep asking you things. I won't ever just tell you.
I'll bring you the ends. Always.

s_mei_vow.say: I had a speech. I've told it to so many people that it's worn out. So. I'll tell you first. Every day, before I tell anybody else. That's the whole vow. It's a big one, for me.

s_bread.dir: She uncovers the loaf, tears it, and tastes it. The square holds still. This is the sentence they will be quoting for a year.

options.text: (The whole square lets out its breath.)

s_crowd.say: Then it is all noise. Eli is coiling her rope with the air of a woman whose form was filled in correctly.

options.text: (Find Noor at the edge of the crowd.)

g_noor.say: Mei will cut it too thick. She always does. It rose well, though. Go on. You've a hall to go home to.

g_tam.say: I'd have paid for lights and a till that sings. My sister baked you a plain loaf and the whole town cried. She's right again. Don't tell her I said so.

g_pip.say: It's called “Proved”. There's a key change where the dough knocks back. It's the first one I've ever sung with my eyes open.

h_mei.say: Two coats. In a hall. I've counted them three times. Right. We're married, the town's been told, and I've nobody left to tell. So, sweetheart. What do we do first?

options.text: Fill the house. I want it loud.
Get rich. Your café, my bread, and then the shop between them.
Get rich. Take the café's lease, sell my bread in it, and then the shop next door.

h_mei_house.say: I grew up four to a room behind a thin wall, and I swore never. Two. And thick walls. And they'll both be told everything, so heaven help the town.

h_mei_rich.say: The old chandler's, next to the café. It's been empty a year, and I know what the company wants for it, because I know everything. We could have it inside the year.

h_mei_sleep.say: Five. You wild thing. All right, love. Five. I'll make the tea at half past.
